So, I booked a museum tour for my kindred to see one of the most fascinating artifacts in the Netherlands: an altar piece for Nehalennia. Most people make the mistake to believe that the Dutch pentagon is the same as the Scandanavian one, with the only difference being the names (Odin is Wodan, Thor is Donar).

However there are some gods and deities who are specifically Dutch, and one of the most important ones is the godess Nehalennia.

The cultus of Nehalennia is thought to be one of the oldes in the Netherlands. The altar of her is over 2000 years old, but she is thought to be worshipped long before that aswell. Altars to her were centered on a very specific location in the Netherlands: on the exact place where the river Schelde flows into the North Sea.

Picture of an Altar stone of Nehalennia in Colijnsplaat Netherlands, depicted with a basket of apples and a dog There were 2 or 3 stone temples devoted to her at that exact place around 2 AD. It was one of the most important trade routes in that time and there have been discoveries in the river that indicate seamen would throw offerings into the river for her when leaving the river by ship (or perhaps when returning safely). This practice was adopted by the romans who copied the exact offering altars one century later in other parts of the Netherlands in the name of Fortuna, godess of luck and fate.

It is believed that Nehalennia was also the godess of fate and some have compared her to the scandinavian Skuld. It probally goes without mentioning that she was also the godess of the sea, or more specifically: the patron of shippers and seamen. She is often depicted with apples, making her a godess of fertility and some of her altars are depicted with a ship's steeringwheel (I don't know the right word for this in English, but you get the point) and a dog.

Nowadays there are two replica temples for Nehalennia. One in the original place where they found the temples and one in a living history museum, where daily sacrifices to this godess are still made and on certain days, different Dutch kindreds meet up there to make an offering.

The altars of Nehalennia are preserved well enough to be able to construct all this information about her, but other altars from 2AD mention Sandraudiga (Godess"red sand"), Vagdavercustis (tree godess) and Viradecdis (unknown godess). These last few godesses presumably only had wooden altar or temple and all information regarding these godesses have been lost when the Roman empire came, even the names of the last two godesses seem to be Latinified germanic. One Roman church was built ontop of a altar of Viradecdis, which is how her name got preserved. It seemed that the southern parts of the Netherlands were rich with different germanic cultusses, but because of the materials (wooden altars and temples) and the Roman empire, most of it is lost.

I hope you enjoyed reading this bit of info and I hope it adds up to a perspective on how diverse the pre-christian germanic religion could be from tribe to tribe and country to country.

Some contemporary info:

If anyone likes metal, the dutch heathen metal band Heidevolk made a song about Nehalennia

Some of the lyrics are: go forth! over the sea's, go forth! Nehalennia A sacrifice made On the Zeeland shore At the altar of the goddess Bringer of wealth Trade and light Show us your favor

There is also this monument in Colijnsplaat. It's a memorial to the "hellish flood" in 1953 where the water was so violent the dykes were breaking and entire parts of the southern Netherlands would get flooded. The village of Colijnsplaat, home of the temple of Nehalennia, was saved against all odds. The village lies in between the river and the sea and had to face the most violent waves from more sides. When the dykes were breaking about 60 people from the village went out into the storm and used their bodies to support the dykes and keeping them from breaking completely. The entire village of Colijnsplaat was saved, the rest of the area was not so lucky: nearly 1800 people met their fate that day. This happened only 60 years ago, showing that the battle against the sea still has a prominent place in the Netherlands and it's no wonder why Nehalennia was such an important godess.
